column8: Play May was a small Special Forces camp in the hills south of Play-koo: twelve American Green Berets, fourteen South Vietnamese, and about four hundred Mon-tan-yard militia, behind a triangle of earth walls and sandbags. On the evening of 19 October, two North Vietnamese regiments moved into position around it. The 33rd would attack the camp. The 32nd would wait beside the road from Play-koo, to ambush the column that would come to save it.

Soon after dark a Mon-tan-yard patrol ran into the enemy, and at midnight the attack began: mortars, recoilless rifles, and waves of infantry against the wire. The defenders held. Through the night and the days that followed, flareships lit the camp and A-one Skyraiders bombed and strafed the attackers close to the walls.

On the morning of 21 October helicopters landed Major Charles Beckwith with a Special Forces reaction team and two companies of South Vietnamese Rangers a few kilometres north-east of the camp. They fought their way in through the jungle and reached the walls. Beckwith took command, and the camp was still surrounded.

Down the road from Play-koo came the relief column: about twelve hundred men under Lieutenant Colonel Nwin Trong Lwat, with M forty-one tanks, M one thirteen armoured carriers, two Ranger battalions and artillery. American guns of the newly arrived 1st Cavalry Division moved forward to cover it. This was the column the 32nd Regiment was waiting for.

In the evening, a few kilometres short of the camp, the 32nd Regiment struck the column from both sides of the road. Tanks and carriers fired back point-blank into the jungle while the American artillery and the aircraft hammered the ambush. The column held, but it stopped where it was, and for a day and a half it would not move.

On the 25th, promised American artillery all the way, Lwat's column pushed on and reached Play May that evening. The North Vietnamese had already begun to pull back west, toward the Choo Pong mountain and the Cambodian border. The camp had held for six days.

General Westmoreland let the 1st Cavalry Division do what it had been built for. Instead of waiting for the enemy, its helicopters went after him. Day after day the brigades leap-frogged west by air, searching the jungle and the grass for the regiments that had attacked Play May.

On 1 November the cavalry found the field hospital of the 33rd Regiment hidden in the forest, and overran it after a hard fight. They took prisoners, weapons and documents, and the documents showed that the enemy regiments were gathering near the Choo Pong.

Two days later the cavalry's own scouts laid an ambush by the Ee-ah Drang near the Cambodian border, and caught a column of a fresh North Vietnamese regiment, the 66th, which had just walked in down the Ho Chi Minh trail. That night the North Vietnamese counter-attacked the little landing zone, and reinforcements were flown in to hold it.

On 9 November the 3rd Brigade took over the hunt. The prisoners and the documents pointed to the Choo Pong, a long forested mountain on the border. On 13 November the brigade commander gave Lieutenant Colonel Hal Moore his orders: take his battalion into the Ee-ah Drang valley, at the foot of the mountain, and find the enemy.

At ten forty-eight on 14 November the first sixteen Hueys came down into a clearing at the foot of the Choo Pong. The clearing was called X-Ray. On the mountain above it were the three battalions of the 66th Regiment and part of the 33rd.
